toc.title: How a defensive state is similar
We need co-regulation, but we're not owed it
You can't talk people into changing

blocks.p: A listener wrote to me with a question that touches three things: autism and the Polyvagal Theory, our partner's defensive state, and how we feel about that. Here's the first part of what she wrote:

q: "Monotone voice, flat affect, etc. My husband is like this always. Autism also displays these characteristics. What is the correlation, please? Is he autistic or just constantly down the ladder?"

blocks.p: I have no idea if her husband would fall on the autism spectrum, and it would be wildly inappropriate for me to diagnose him or give my thoughts on him in particular. So I'm speaking generally here, not to her or to you specifically.

There is potentially a polyvagal connection to autism, and it's something Dr. Porges has written about. I don't consider myself an autism expert whatsoever. I have a very light understanding of it. People are often surprised that therapy school doesn't teach trauma and Polyvagal Theory in depth, and likewise, we get some education on the autism spectrum, but not a whole lot, in my opinion. A lot of it is what we learn after school.
Here's a direct quote from Porges:

q: "Observations of the behaviors and physiologic response of autistic individuals suggest that they have great difficulties in recruiting the neural circuit that regulates the social engagement system."

blocks.p: And on top of that:

q: "Because the vagus is integrated into several feedback systems involving both peripheral and central structures, depression or dysregulation of the vagus might be manifested on several levels."

blocks.p: Let me interpret that as best I can. The first part is saying that autistic individuals could have a difficult time accessing their ventral vagal safety state. The second part is saying that the vagus is connected to so many things that if there's dysregulation through the vagus, we would see dysregulation in different aspects of someone on the autism spectrum. Not just social. I think we often associate autism with the sociability aspect, but there's potentially much more.

blocks.h: How a defensive state is similar

blocks.p: Someone in a state of defense has less access to their safety state. That's true for me, you, anybody. If we're down our [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), we simply have less access to safety. That's potentially very similar for someone with autism.

But the potential for self-regulation seems to be different. Again, I'm not an expert, but there seems to be a big difference in the potential for climbing our own ladder. Someone who's not on the spectrum can go into a defensive state day to day and then get back up to their safety state. They can self-regulate through it, or receive co-regulation, and it's really not a big deal. Someone on the autism spectrum simply has less access to their safety state, and it seems like chronically.

And the safety state isn't just for socializing. That's where critical thinking happens. That's where health and growth and restoration happen. A lot comes along with being in our ventral vagal state of safety and social engagement.
It's obviously not that simple. Autism has other characteristics that aren't part of a typical down-the-ladder individual. According to Autism Speaks, people with autism may have:

ul: Challenges with spoken language. A third of autistic people are non-verbal. Someone in a defensive state, even a stuck one, isn't necessarily going to have issues using language.
Repetitive body movements, like rocking, flapping, spinning, or running back and forth.
Repetitive motions with objects, like spinning wheels, shaking sticks, or flipping levers.
Staring at lights or spinning objects.
Ritualistic behaviors, like lining up objects or repeatedly touching objects in a set order.
Narrow or extreme interests in specific topics.
A need for unvarying routine and resistance to change: the same daily schedule, meal menu, clothes, the same route to school.
Sensory issues, like being over or under-sensitive to lights.

blocks.p: These aren't necessarily aspects of someone in a defensive state, stuck or not. For someone on the spectrum, it sounds like these are day in, day out aspects of life.
There are similarities with someone in a defensive state: tone of voice, eye contact, socialization, emotional expression, being overwhelmed in social situations, talking over others.

Someone in a defensive state has less access to their vocal prosody, that singsongy quality of the voice. Someone in flight and anxiety might have more of a high pitch. They'll make less eye contact. They'll socialize less. They'll have less emotional expression, and their affect might even go flat, whether they're temporarily in a defensive state or stuck there. They might be easily overwhelmed in social situations, because they're really not ready to socially engage when they're down the ladder. And they might talk over others.

But with autism, I don't think it's an aggressive thing. If you're in flight or fight, it's going to be more anxiety-ridden or aggressive. It's more than just missing social cues. There's aggression to it, there's dominance.

So are there similarities? Sure. Is being on the spectrum the same thing as being stuck in a defensive state, or temporarily in one that you can self-regulate out of? No. These are worlds apart. The idea from Dr. Porges is that someone on the spectrum simply has less capacity to access their ventral safety and social engagement state. Those pathways are harder to activate and harder to stay in.

Porges's Safe and Sound Protocol uses sound that's designed to be more prosodic, to, quote unquote, "stimulate" the vagus nerve, or at least the safety pathways. Prosody is a cue of safety for any of us, and it helps us climb our ladders. It's been used with people on the autism spectrum, and from what Porges reports, there's been a lot of success there.
When I talked with him years later, he shared one moment from his early work with autistic children:

q: "One totally... previously dysregulated child who couldn't even have headset on. He was so sensitive, ran into this sound attenuating chamber I built, which had speakers in it and said, with his limited vocabulary, one word: 'Safe.'"
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [From Sound to Safety: Understanding the Safe & Sound Protocol (episode 254)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/20b541da-11ef-4b2e-b911-42b6ceba2bd1)

blocks.p: So is access to the ventral state completely gone in autism? I don't know, but it seems like no. It seems like there's potential for those ventral pathways to be active, and to experience some social engagement, connection, and safety, at least in that moment. I couldn't tell you how long-lasting or permanent that is. I don't think it's an issue of a cure. But that's the potential connection. And again, autism and a defensive state, stuck or temporary, are very different.
This is where my mind went with the question, regardless of all of that: let's not diagnose our partners.

Maybe Polyvagal Theory gives us an explanation for who we are, and for who our spouses are. Okay, fine. Maybe that gives us a sense of understanding them, even a sense of predictability, and maybe you can use that to try to help. But it's also potentially just a label we can now fling at our significant others, our families, our friends.

This stuff can be used just like a DSM diagnosis, inappropriately. When you're in your own aggressive fight state and trying to communicate with your significant other, "You're a jerk. Go get help," might come out of your mouth. Or, "You're a narcissist. Go get help." That's a diagnosis, but it can be used wildly inappropriately. And you could just as easily say, "You're in your fight state, you jerk. Go get help." They're not the same thing, but the intent is.

Whether it's a diagnosis or a spot on the polyvagal ladder, it can easily become part of judgment and blame. The beauty of the Polyvagal Theory is that there's no judgment to it. It just is. It's a new paradigm for viewing ourselves and building a new narrative for ourselves. There's no inherent value, no judgment, no blame. But you can take it and weaponize it in arguments with people you care about.

So I'd encourage all of us to stay away from diagnosing the people we care about, whether through the DSM, through the polyvagal ladder, or through calling people names like jerk and asshole. Call it a label rather than a diagnosis. No matter what your paradigm for labeling somebody is, it can be weaponized. The message is: you're the problem. You have the diagnosis. You're abnormal. You're not treating me right. There's something wrong with you.

As a therapist, applying Polyvagal Theory to others is what I do. It has its uses on a professional level, absolutely. As a parent, I use it with my kids. And I use it in my marriage as well. But the angle is: where am I on my polyvagal ladder? How much co-regulation am I able to give somebody? Not, "You're the problem. This is where you're at. Fix yourself." It's me. I apply it to myself and build myself a new narrative. I put the responsibility on myself to do what I can as part of this dyad, which will hopefully help the other person, or the family as a whole. But myself first.

blocks.h: We need co-regulation, but we're not owed it

blocks.p: The listener went on:

q: "I have been triggered by it constantly. You are the first to explain it. A million thanks. Please, please, please reply. I have suffered so much over the years, and I have asked him infinite times to not be monotonous and to smile, etc. And you're the first person to ever back me up."

blocks.p: I can validate the need for co-regulation. All of us have this need. And co-regulation doesn't simply mean we support each other, or that our partner supports us. That could be what it looks like on a behavioral level. But co-regulation is a biological communication happening between two nervous systems, two mammals, two people. It's cues of safety that one nervous system sends to the other. So one of them has to be in their safe and social state, or have enough access to it, to provide cues of safety.

We all need co-regulation from our loved ones, our families, our coworkers. My voice in your ears right now: you need me to be a co-regulator just because we're both mammals. If I were yelling at you, I don't think your system would like that. Ideally I have enough vocal prosody and you pick that up. We all need things like a safe voice, gentle touch, eye crinkles and eyebrows that move, and the ability to tilt our head and listen. I validate that 100%.

However, and this is where I want to take it, we are not owed it, and we are not entitled to it. It's not up to other people to give us co-regulation. I think it's a good idea for all of us to provide safety cues to each other. But I don't expect that from anybody. I hope for it. I'd love it. I'd appreciate it. But it's out of my hands.

I'm not owed that from you. I'm not entitled to it. I can hope for it. I'll send mine to you, but that's a decision I make. Or debatably, the decision I make is to be in a safe and social state, and once I'm self-regulated enough, I send safety cues naturally. I'd hope all of us are doing the same, but that's out of my hands. I can't demand it from you, even though I need it. We all do, because we're mammals.
So it's not up to us to demand co-regulation from others. But it is up to us to find people in our lives who are able to give it to us.

I'd love it if everybody in your life were in their safe and social state and offering you co-regulation. That may not be the reality. Especially once you're aware of this, look at the people you allow into your life as a choice you're making. If someone new isn't self-regulated enough, you're allowed to say no. For the people who are already there, creating healthy boundaries is a really good idea. But expecting them to be what they are not isn't fair to them, I don't think.

Co-regulation doesn't come from demanding it. If you're demanding that someone smile at you, or pleading or begging them to, I don't know if whatever you get back is a genuine smile. I don't know if that's genuine co-regulation.

It is, of course, okay to tell people what you need. "I need you to be more sensitive, more empathetic. I need you to understand me. I need you to care." Yes, of course you do. It's 100% okay to express that, and that's different from demanding it or expecting it. Hopefully you have people in your life who say, "I care about you, and I'll make these changes." Basically you're saying, "I need people in my life who are self-regulated enough to be safe people to surround myself with." Hopefully the people in your life are invested in their own self-regulation and wellbeing, not exactly for you, but as a priority of their own.

But ultimately, someone can say no. Maybe it comes from a defensive state. It doesn't matter. We don't control people. They do with themselves what they choose to do. We can debate whether that's free will, but it at least looks like choice. I know this is obvious, but I don't think it hurts to remind us.
So:

ul: Can we express what we need from others? Hell yeah.
Can we allow people into our lives who fulfill what we need? Yep.
Can we remove people from our lives who don't fit what we need? Yes.
Can we create healthy boundaries with the ones we keep? Absolutely. It might be hard, but we can.

blocks.p: What I'd encourage all of us to do is to be self-regulated first, and then provide co-regulation. That might seem backwards. We need co-regulation, at least as children, to build the ability to self-regulate. We always need co-regulation, but as children, hopefully we got enough to build self-regulation.

Some of you may be thinking, "I didn't get that. I'm not very well self-regulated. I need it from other people." That's true. But it also might not happen, and it may be more realistic to take ownership of your self-regulation instead of waiting for others to provide co-regulation. I don't know if you have those people in your life. What you do have is you. And you have this knowledge of Polyvagal Theory. You can say, "I'm going to take ownership of my self-regulation, and not expect it of others, but I will be looking for it."

Be self-regulated first, and you'll naturally provide co-regulation to others. And what's really cool is you'll attract people who can do the same. I find that people in a very dysregulated place find others in a very dysregulated place, and people who are fairly self-regulated find people who are fairly self-regulated. Like attracts like.

So get anchored in your safety state as much as you can, and you'll naturally send cues of safety to the people in your life. And the people who need to get to the top of their ladders are probably more likely to get there from your safety cues than if you demanded it from them. You being self-regulated and offering cues of safety is probably more helpful than you being dysregulated, demanding it, and guilt-tripping people about not giving you what you need.

blocks.h: You can't talk people into changing

blocks.p: This comes up in therapy a lot, with my clients of every age, adults and kids and teens. Yes, we have needs. But we don't control people. We can't demand it. Let me repeat that: we cannot talk people into changing, I don't think.

We can set up healthy boundaries, positive expectations, negative consequences. We can say, "You're not a part of my life until you make a change." But that's more about us making choices for ourselves. I don't think you can reason people into changing. They have to be at least open to it in the first place. A lot of the people I work with say, "I tell them this, and I tell them this, and I tell them this." And does it help? No, because we don't control other people.

Yes, you need co-regulation. Yes, I need co-regulation. I don't expect you to give it to me. I hope you would, but I'm going to do the best I can to give it to you and to everybody else I can. That starts with me being as self-regulated as I possibly can, and I hope you'd make that same commitment. If enough of us do that, I think it's a much different world.

I find more satisfaction in my friendships, my relationships, and myself as a parent the more work I do on my own self-regulation. And I find myself needing less from other people. I still need them. I need my wife. I need my kids. Of course. I'm not saying, "I'm good on my own now." But the amount of need just isn't as intense. I'm more okay, I'm more patient, I'm more empathetic, and I just need less from other people in that way.
Whatever we want in life, to improve our relationships, our outcomes, to meet new goals, it always starts and ends with us, in my opinion.

I am responsible for my state. Nobody else is. My wife is not responsible for my state. My kids aren't, my boss isn't, my coworkers aren't. We all affect each other, yes. My parents affected me growing up. My friends affected me then, and my friends now. It's like a web of cues of safety and danger. True. But in this chaotic web of safety and danger cues, I'm the constant. No matter who's in or out of my life, I'm the common denominator of my life. You're the common denominator of yours. So it always has to start with you, for your life.

I'll put it this way: I'm responsible for making change to my state. Someone who affects our state in a very negative way bears responsibility, I would argue. But when it comes to getting out of a stuck defensive state, when it comes to making change in our own lives, that's on us. That's the caveat.

So when it comes to our partners and spouses, yes, we need things from them. I hope they're willing to work with you, but they might not be, and that's out of our control. So the question becomes: it's your life, these are the people in it, what's the next step? What are you going to do about it?

Be as self-regulated as possible, and then answer that question, because if you answer it from a fight state, it might not be a good answer. Get as regulated as you can, and then say, "This is who is in my life. This is how they are. I can't control them. I can't force them to be the way I want them to be. So what's my next step? What am I going to do about it?" That's really it.
